visual.title: Inspection
visual.goal: Find visible damage before measuring or powering anything.

steps.text: **Unplug the power** and take out any batteries.
**Light the area well** and use a magnifier or your phone's camera zoomed in.

**Look for:** burn marks or brown patches, a bulged or leaking capacitor top, cracks in a part's body, green or white crust (corrosion), solder bridging two pins, a dull or cracked joint, a lifted pin, a loose wire.
**Smell it.** A burnt smell close to a part points to it.

visual.limits: Most failed parts look perfectly normal. Finding nothing proves nothing.

answers.label: I see damage (say where in the notes)

rail-to-ground.title: Rail to ground: is it shorted?
rail-to-ground.goal: One reading tells whether anything on this supply rail is shorted to ground. Every capacitor on the rail is in parallel, so a clean reading clears all of them of a short at once.

steps.text: **Unplug the power** and wait a minute for the capacitors to discharge.
**Meter on Ω (resistance)**, not the beeper. **Touch the two probes together** and note the reading: the leads' own resistance.

**Black probe on ground, red probe on the rail**, at the points the step shows. Hold them still for **five seconds**: the reading often starts low and climbs as the capacitors charge. Note it once it stops moving.

expect.text: Climbs past 1 kΩ, or to OL. On a small 5 V board, under 10 Ω and steady is a fault.

rail-to-ground.limits: Clears the rail's capacitors of a short only: not an open or worn capacitor, not a dead chip that is not shorted.

answers.label: Under 1 Ω and steady: a hard short
Over 1 kΩ, or climbing to OL

continuity.title: Continuity between two points
continuity.goal: Whether two points are connected by copper. Also how the board model's connections become measured.

steps.text: **Unplug the power.**
**Meter on Ω**, not the beeper (meters beep up to 10 to 200 Ω, which hides a bad joint). Touch the probes together and note the leads' resistance.
**One probe on each point** the step shows, pressing on the solder, not the varnish. Note the reading.

expect.text: Under 2 Ω when connected by copper; OL when not. Anything in between goes through a part.

answers.label: 2 Ω to 100 kΩ: through a part
Over 100 kΩ or OL: not connected

rail-voltage.title: Rail voltage, powered
rail-voltage.goal: Whether a supply rail is at its voltage, measured where it is used.

steps.text: **Meter on DC volts** (V with a straight line). Clip or hold the **black probe on ground** before powering.
**Plug the power in** and switch the unit on. Keep your hand off the board except for the red probe.
**Red probe on the point the step shows.** Hold it steady; don't let it slip onto a neighbouring pin.
**Unplug the power** before moving on.

rail-voltage.limits: A multimeter shows an average: it cannot see a dip lasting a few milliseconds, such as the one behind a reset when a motor starts.

current-draw.title: Current drawn from the supply
current-draw.goal: The board's current at idle and during one action. The pattern sorts the fault: none, a little, too much, or pulsing.

steps.text: **Put the USB power meter between the adapter and the unit's cable.**
**Switch the unit on** and wait until it is idle. Note the current.
**Do the action the step names once**, watching the meter. Note the highest current you see, and anything odd (it drops to 0, it pulses).

current-draw.limits: A USB meter updates a few times a second: it misses very short spikes.

resistor.title: Resistor: value
resistor.goal: A resistor fails open or drifts high far more often than it shorts. On the board, other parts in parallel can only lower the reading: a reading above the marked value is real, a lower one is not proof.

steps.text: **Unplug the power.** Read the marking: 3 digits (`472` = 47 × 10² = 4.7 kΩ), 4 digits (`1002` = 10 kΩ), or `R` for the decimal point (`R390` = 0.39 Ω).
**Look at it:** a charred or cracked body, or a discoloured board under it.
**Meter on Ω.** Touch the probes together and note the leads' resistance (matters under 10 Ω).
**One probe on each end** of the resistor. Note the reading once it settles.

resistor.limits: In circuit, a reading below the marked value is not a fault by itself: lift one end to be sure.

capacitor.title: Ceramic capacitor: short
capacitor.goal: Ceramic capacitors fail shorted, often from a crack you cannot see. A meter tells shorted from not shorted; not the value.

steps.text: **Unplug the power** and wait a minute.
**Look at it** under a magnifier: a crack across the body, or a chip at its ends.
**Meter on Ω, one probe on each end.** The reading climbs as it charges. Note it after five seconds.

capacitor.limits: On the board this reads the same as the whole rail it sits on: a short here may be any part on that rail.

electrolytic.title: Electrolytic capacitor: look and short
electrolytic.goal: Electrolytics mostly wear out (their ESR rises), which a multimeter cannot see. It can find a shorted one and show the visible signs.

steps.text: **Unplug the power.** Meter on DC volts across it (red on `+`, the side without the stripe): under 0.5 V before touching. Higher: discharge it through a 1 kΩ resistor.
**Look at the top and the base:** a domed top, brown crust or a stained board around it is a failed capacitor.
**Meter on Ω, red on `+`, black on `-`.** The reading should climb towards high values as it charges. Note it after ten seconds.

electrolytic.limits: A pass clears it of a short only. A worn capacitor (high ESR) reads normal here: only an ESR meter, or temporarily fitting a good one in parallel, can tell.

electrolytic-esr.title: Electrolytic capacitor: ESR
electrolytic-esr.goal: The ESR (internal resistance) is how worn an electrolytic is, and it can be measured on the board.

steps.text: **Unplug the power** and check it is discharged (under 0.5 V).
**Clip the ESR meter across it**, polarity as marked on the meter. Note the ESR.

expect.text: At or below the chart value for its capacitance and voltage (47 µF 16 V: 2 Ω, 100 µF 16 V: 0.7 Ω, 470 µF 16 V: 0.2 Ω). Two to three times that is worn.

answers.label: At or below the chart value
Two times the chart value or more

diode.title: Diode: junction test
diode.goal: A diode conducts one way only. The meter's diode mode shows its forward voltage one way and OL the other.

steps.text: **Unplug the power.** Meter on diode mode (the diode symbol).
**Forward:** red probe on the anode, black on the cathode (the end with the band).
**Reverse:** swap the probes.

expect.text: 0.5 to 0.8 V forward (0.15 to 0.45 V for a Schottky), OL reverse.

diode.limits: In circuit, a part in parallel can lower both readings. A low reading both ways needs one end lifted to be sure.

answers.label: A junction one way, OL the other

led.title: LED: junction test
led.goal: An LED is a diode with a higher forward voltage. Most meters make a red, green or yellow LED glow faintly in diode mode.

steps.text: **Unplug the power.** Meter on diode mode.
**Forward:** red probe on the anode (the longer leg, or the side without the mark), black on the cathode. Watch whether it glows.
**Reverse:** swap the probes.

expect.text: Red, yellow and green: 1.5 to 2.2 V forward, often a faint glow. Blue and white: 2.6 to 3.5 V, which some meters cannot reach (they show OL). OL reverse.

bjt.title: Bipolar transistor: junctions
bjt.goal: A bipolar transistor is two diodes sharing the base. Exactly two of the six readings conduct, both through the base, and collector to emitter never does.

steps.text: **Unplug the power.** Meter on diode mode. Find B, C and E from the pinout (SOT-23 is usually 1 = B, 2 = E, 3 = C).
**Base to emitter:** NPN: red on the base, black on the emitter (PNP: the other way).
**Base to collector:** same polarity, black on the collector.
**Swap the probes on both junctions:** both should read OL. Note the lowest.
**Collector to emitter, both ways.** Note the lowest.

expect.text: 0.5 to 0.8 V on both junctions forward, OL reversed, OL collector to emitter.
expect.source: Kuphaldt, Meter check of a transistor

bjt.limits: In circuit this is a screen: a base resistor or a load in parallel can lower the readings.

answers.label: A junction reads under 0.1 V: shorted

mosfet.title: MOSFET: body diode and gate
mosfet.goal: A MOSFET shows one diode (its body diode) between source and drain, and nothing at all at its gate.

steps.text: **Unplug the power.** Meter on diode mode. Touch gate and source together with a probe tip to discharge the gate.
**Body diode:** N-channel: red on the source, black on the drain (P-channel: the other way).
**Drain to source, the other way.**
**Gate to drain and gate to source, both ways.** Note the lowest.

expect.text: Body diode 0.4 to 0.9 V, OL the other way, OL from the gate.

answers.label: Drain to source low both ways: shorted
Body diode one way, the rest OL

inductor.title: Inductor or ferrite: continuity
inductor.goal: An inductor is a coil: it reads a low resistance end to end. It fails open.

steps.text: **Unplug the power.** Meter on Ω; touch the probes together and note the leads.
**One probe on each end.**

expect.text: Power inductors and ferrite beads: under 1 Ω. Through-hole chokes: 1 to 50 Ω.

inductor.limits: A shorted turn or a cracked core still reads fine: it needs an LCR meter.

switch.title: Switch or button: contacts
switch.goal: A switch must read near 0 Ω when closed and open when released, steadily.

steps.text: **Unplug the power.** Meter on Ω, one probe on each contact.
**Released (or OFF):** note the reading. On the board it may read the circuit around it instead of OL.
**Pressed (or ON):** hold it and note the reading. Press several times: it should be steady.

answers.label: Near 0 Ω even when released: stuck closed
Pressed reads over 10 Ω: worn or dirty contacts

ic-pins.title: Integrated circuit: supply and output pins
ic-pins.goal: A meter cannot prove a chip works, but a shorted supply or output stage shows up. Compare pins of the same kind with each other.

steps.text: **Unplug the power.** Find pin 1 (a dot or dimple; pins count anticlockwise seen from above) and the datasheet's supply, ground and output pins.
**Look at it:** a crack or bulge in the package, a burn mark, bridged or lifted pins.
**Supply to ground:** meter on Ω, black on a ground pin, red on the supply pin. Wait for the reading to settle.
**Each output pin to ground and to the supply pin, both probe directions.** Note the lowest reading.

ic-pins.limits: No short found does not mean the chip works.

wire.title: Wire or pad: continuity
wire.goal: Check a wire and its joint end to end, and that it does not touch its neighbours.

steps.text: **Unplug the power.** Look at the joint: dull, cracked or balled solder, broken strands at the pad.
**Meter on Ω, one probe on the pad, the other on the wire's far end.** Wiggle the wire while watching.
**This pad to the next pad or wire.**

answers.label: Over 2 Ω, or it flickers: broken

motor.title: DC motor: winding
motor.goal: A small brushed motor reads a few ohms at every position of its shaft. Open at one position is a worn brush or a broken winding; near 0 everywhere is a short.

steps.text: **Unplug the power and disconnect the motor** from the board (both wires).
**Meter on Ω across the motor's two terminals.** Turn the shaft slowly by hand through a full turn, watching the reading. Note the lowest.
**And the highest** you saw during the turn.

motor.limits: Brush contact makes the meter read high; a single shorted turn does not show.

fuse.title: Fuse: continuity
fuse.goal: A fuse is a wire: near 0 Ω when good, open when blown. A blown fuse is a symptom: something downstream drew too much.

steps.text: **Unplug the power.** Meter on Ω, one probe on each end.
